newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: FEATURE-Namibia seeks truth to purge past.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Namibia seeks truth to purge past.

text.p: The summer wind sweeping Namibia's Kalahari sands is blowing a political storm in the vast southern African desert state, uncovering the bare bones of war dead.

President Sam Nujoma's government -- which came to power six years ago after a bloody guerrilla war for independence from apartheid South Africa -- is engaged in a bitter battle over charges that its SWAPO party committed atrocities during the 23 year-long conflict.
Some critics are demanding that Namibia establish a South African-type "truth commission" to determine exactly what happened at the time.

Namibia, a huge, empty country of just 1.5 million people, is being rocked by shockwaves from a book, published last year, by Siegfried Groth, a pastor of the German Lutheran Church who lived and worked for years in South West Africa, as the country was known before independence in 1990.

Groth was actively involved in SWAPO's independence struggle. In "Namibia: The Wall of Silence" he claims thousands of thousands of SWAPO members branded dissidents by their own top leaders were tortured or killed between 1974 and 1979.
The abuses took place at SWAPO military camps in neighbouring Zambia and Angola, Groth says.

Groth says he wrote the book not out of malice, because he generally admires SWAPO and Nujoma's leadership before and after independence. His declared aim is to help Namibia deal with its ugly past so that it can "avoid the disasters of radical tribalism that continues to be a threat to the new nation".

But the book has plunged the sleepy former German and later South African colony into its most lively political debate in six years, dominating television and radio airwaves and filling up independent and official newspaper columns.

The government has published its own volume -- "Their Blood Waters Our Freedom" -- defending SWAPO's record, and accusing its critics of trying to shift blame onto the party instead of South Africa's ex-apartheid regime.
South Africa's former white rulers have acknowledged their army killed thousands of innocent Namibians, the SWAPO history says.

Namibian Prime Minister Hage Geingob admits some SWAPO cadres were killed in inter-factional struggles or after being wrongly labelled South African spies. But he says many of those alleged by Groth to have been murdered in fact died as heroes on the war front.

Gwen Lister, editor of the leading independent daily newspaper The Namibian, says both the government and parties, including the main opposition Democratic Turnhalle Alliance which backed the former authorities in Pretoria in the fight against independence, should acknowledge their dirty past.

"They would do well to admit their wrongdoings to the people of Namibia so that we can put the past behind us and get on with building a secure future for all. Sometimes a simple apology can clear the way," she said.

But war veterans in a SWAPO-dominated parliament see no need for an apology from their party or for a "truth commission." They are threatening instead to press for war crimes trials for their old foes such as those under way for Bosnia and Rwanda.
"You must account for what you did," an angry SWAPO member Hadino Hishongwa told opposition MPs during a recent, heated parliamentary debate.
Nahas Angula, an ex-SWAPO guerrilla commander who is now Namibia's minister of higher education, endorses that demand.

"At the end of the day, if push comes to shove, the people of Namibia have a right to demand the establishment of an international tribunal to try the crimes of apartheid and illegal occupation," Angula said.

The Windhoek Advertiser, another main daily newspaper, says Namibians must look themselves straight in the mirror, and see their blemishes. But the paper fears any "truth commission" here could be manipulated by the government.
"The truth will set us free as the saying goes, but the truth by commission will deliver us into bondage," it commented.
The Namibian National Society for Human Rights has, through its outspoken executive director Phil ya Nangoloh, also been urging all parties to come clean on alleged atrocities.
Its position is generally supported by the Christian Council of Namibia, which plans to convene a public forum on the issue later this year.
But CCN President Landespropst Keding also opposes the setting up of a commission, on the grounds that it would not help the process of reconciliation.

Keding says the current debate should not go beyond establishing the exact stories of those who suffered alleged human rights violations, clearing those falsely accused of spying or treason, and extracting some form of apology to those who suffered at the hands of their own comrades during the war.
